Imputed mean and SD of one study, with their plug-in standard errors

Source: R/se_imputed.R
se_imputed.Rd

The study-level wrapper for practitioners: give it a study's reported values and sample size, and it returns the imputed mean \(\hat\mu\) and SD \(\hat\sigma\), the naive standard error \(\hat\sigma/\sqrt n\) that treats \(\hat\mu\) as a sample mean, and the plug-in standard errors \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\mu) = C_\mu(n)\,\hat\sigma\) and \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat\sigma) = C_\sigma(n)\,\hat\sigma\) built from the normal-model factors of c_mu and c_sigma. The default estimator version is the BLUE (Lloyd's least-squares estimators from the reported values, the exact-optimal version of the Wan-Luo-Shi estimators); version = "wan_luo_shi" gives the estimators of Wan, Luo and Shi (Luo's mean, Wan's SD under S1 and S2, Shi's under S3, with their closed-form weights and the Blom formulas) and their own factors. Both are computed exactly at every sample size.

Usage

se_imputed(
  q,
  n,
  scenario = c("S3", "S1", "S2", "S4", "S5"),
  version = c("blue", "wan_luo_shi"),
  type = 7
)

# S3 method for class 'se_imputed'
print(x, digits = 4L, ...)

Arguments

q

Named numeric vector of the reported values: min, med, max for S1; q1, med, q3 for S2; all five (min, q1, med, q3, max) for S3; p10, q1, med, q3, p90 for S4; and min, p10, q1, med, q3, p90, max for S5, where p10 and p90 are the 10th and 90th percentiles. Extra names are ignored, a required name given twice is an error, and the entries used must be non-decreasing.

n

Integer sample size: at least 3 under S1 and S2, 5 under S3 and S4, and 7 under S5.

scenario

One of "S1" to "S5".

version

"blue" (default) or "wan_luo_shi".

type

The definition of the reported sample quantiles, an integer from 1 to 9 as in quantile; 7, R's default, unless the study states another. See Details.

x

An object returned by se_imputed().

digits

The number of significant digits the print shows.

...

Passed to print.default for the estimates.

Value

An object of class "se_imputed": a list, used as any list, whose print shows the estimates, the standard errors and the factors. Its components: mu_hat, sigma_hat, se_naive \(= \hat\sigma/\sqrt n\), se_mu \(= C_\mu(n)\hat\sigma\), se_sigma \(= C_\sigma(n)\hat\sigma\), the factors c_n and c_sigma used, exact (TRUE: the factors are computed exactly, at every \(n\)), version and version_used (the same, kept for the columns of se_imputed_df), plus n, scenario, type and the weights w_mean, w_sd, named by the reported values as estimator_weights names them (a the minimum, m the median, b the maximum, q1, q3, p10, p90). The example shows how to pick the fields a meta-analysis needs.

Details

The sample size. At \(n = 4Q + 1\) with integer \(Q \ge 1\), under the default definition (type 7), the reported quartiles are the order statistics at ranks \(Q+1, 2Q+1, 3Q+1\). At any other \(n\), each reported sample quantile is a fixed linear combination of two adjacent order statistics, and the estimators and their factors are computed exactly from the means and covariance matrix of the reported values (see imputed_moments). At such \(n\) the factors depend on the definition of the sample quantiles; the median of an even sample is the average of the two middle values under type 7 (and types 2, 5, 6, 8 and 9).

The shortcut formulas for the factors (c_mu_shortcut, c_sigma_shortcut) are not used here. They serve a reader without this package and a comparison with the exact values.

Under S4 and S5 only the BLUE is defined; version = "wan_luo_shi" is an error there.

A constant summary, all reported values equal, has an imputed SD of exactly zero (the SD weights sum to zero) and so standard errors of zero, which cannot enter inverse-variance weights. The function returns them with a warning; se_imputed_df sets such a row to NA instead.

Assumptions: iid normal data. The standard errors are plug-in quantities, \(\sigma\) being replaced by \(\hat\sigma\); their reference distribution is not Student's t and is not supplied here.

Examples

r <- se_imputed(c(q1 = 10, med = 12, q3 = 15), n = 25, scenario = "S2")
r                                        # the compact print
#> Imputed mean and SD under S2, n = 25, the BLUE, quantile type 7
#>    mu_hat sigma_hat  se_naive     se_mu  se_sigma 
#>   12.3575    3.9252    0.7850    0.8442    0.9311 
#> Factors: C_mu(n) = 0.2151, C_sigma(n) = 0.2372. The weights are $w_mean and $w_sd; every field with str() or unclass().
r[c("mu_hat", "se_mu")]                  # the fields a meta-analysis needs, as a list
#> $mu_hat
#> [1] 12.35747
#> 
#> $se_mu
#> [1] 0.8441742
#> 
se_imputed(c(q1 = 10, med = 12, q3 = 15), n = 25, scenario = "S2", version = "wan_luo_shi")
#> Imputed mean and SD under S2, n = 25, the Wan-Luo-Shi estimators, quantile type 7
#>    mu_hat sigma_hat  se_naive     se_mu  se_sigma 
#>   12.3578    3.9306    0.7861    0.8453    0.9337 
#> Factors: C_mu(n) = 0.2151, C_sigma(n) = 0.2375. The weights are $w_mean and $w_sd; every field with str() or unclass().
se_imputed(c(q1 = 10, med = 12, q3 = 15), n = 24, scenario = "S2")   # interpolated quartiles
#> Imputed mean and SD under S2, n = 24, the BLUE, quantile type 7
#>    mu_hat sigma_hat  se_naive     se_mu  se_sigma 
#>   12.3634    3.9285    0.8019    0.8544    0.9224 
#> Factors: C_mu(n) = 0.2175, C_sigma(n) = 0.2348. The weights are $w_mean and $w_sd; every field with str() or unclass().
se_imputed(c(min = 3, q1 = 10, med = 12, q3 = 15, max = 30), n = 30, "S3")
#> Imputed mean and SD under S3, n = 30, the BLUE, quantile type 7
#>    mu_hat sigma_hat  se_naive     se_mu  se_sigma 
#>   12.9405    5.6194    1.0260    1.0591    0.8176 
#> Factors: C_mu(n) = 0.1885, C_sigma(n) = 0.1455. The weights are $w_mean and $w_sd; every field with str() or unclass().
